name: Mask of Tutankhamun
subtitle: Royal funerary mask
material: Gold, glass and semi-precious stones (lapis lazuli, carnelian, turquoise)
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Found in 1922 by Howard Carter's excavation team inside the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62).
description: This gold funerary mask was placed over the head of the mummified king and is one of the most recognizable surviving works of ancient Egyptian art. It combines idealized royal portraiture with the protective imagery of Egyptian burial practice.
significance: The mask demonstrates the craftsmanship, symbolism, and royal funerary traditions of the New Kingdom, and became a global symbol of ancient Egypt after the tomb's discovery.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Rosetta Stone
subtitle: Trilingual inscribed stela
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Found in 1799 by French soldiers during the Napoleonic campaign in Egypt, near the town of Rosetta.
description: The stone bears a decree issued at Memphis, written in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek.
significance: Because the same text appears in three scripts, the stone was the key that allowed Jean-François Champollion to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

name: Bust of Nefertiti
subtitle: Royal portrait sculpture
origin: Workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, Amarna
location: Neues Museum, Berlin
discovery: Excavated in 1912 by a German archaeological team led by Ludwig Borchardt at Amarna.
description: A painted bust traditionally identified as Queen Nefertiti, showing the refined naturalism associated with the Amarna period under Akhenaten.
significance: The bust is renowned for its craftsmanship and has become one of the most reproduced images of ancient Egyptian art.

name: Seated Scribe
subtitle: Painted limestone statue
material: Painted limestone, inlaid eyes of rock crystal and copper
location: Musée du Louvre, Paris
discovery: Excavated in 1893 during French archaeological work at Saqqara.
description: A painted limestone figure of a seated scribe holding a partially unrolled papyrus, a common type of Old Kingdom tomb statue meant to preserve the image of an official for eternity.
significance: The lifelike inlaid eyes and careful modeling make it one of the best-known examples of Old Kingdom private statuary.

name: Great Sphinx of Giza
subtitle: Monumental guardian statue
location: Giza Plateau, in situ
discovery: Never fully lost to history, though it was partly buried in sand for long periods and cleared in several campaigns, most notably in the early 20th century.
description: A colossal limestone figure with the body of a lion and a human head, generally associated with King Khafre, carved from the natural bedrock of the Giza Plateau.
significance: It is one of the largest and oldest monumental sculptures in the world and forms part of the royal funerary landscape of Giza.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Canopic Jar of Imsety
subtitle: Funerary vessel for preserved organs
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Recovered from New Kingdom burial contexts at Thebes; part of a set of four jars, each protected by one of the Four Sons of Horus.
description: Canopic jars held the internal organs removed during mummification. Each of the four jars in a set was associated with a different protective deity.
significance: They reflect the religious beliefs surrounding preservation of the body and provision for the afterlife.

name: Scarab Amulet
subtitle: Protective seal amulet
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Scarabs of this type are known from tombs and settlement sites across Middle Kingdom Egypt.
description: Modeled on the dung beetle, scarab amulets and seals were worn or placed in burials and often carved with inscriptions on the flat underside.
significance: The scarab was linked to the god Khepri and ideas of transformation and rebirth, and became one of the most common amulet forms in Egyptian material culture.

name: Narmer Palette
subtitle: Ceremonial siltstone palette
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Excavated in 1897–1898 by James Quibell at the temple site of Hierakonpolis.
description: A ceremonial cosmetic palette carved in low relief with scenes generally interpreted as showing King Narmer asserting authority over Upper and Lower Egypt.
significance: It is a key source for understanding early Egyptian kingship, iconography, and the political unification associated with the start of the dynastic era.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Naqada II Painted Vessel
subtitle: Decorated pottery jar
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Vessels of this type come from Predynastic cemetery excavations in Upper Egypt beginning in the late 19th century.
description: A buff-ware jar painted with reddish-brown depictions of boats, animals, and geometric bands, typical of Naqada II pottery traditions.
significance: These vessels illustrate the artistic and social developments of Predynastic Nile Valley communities before Egypt's unification.

name: Ripple-Flaked Flint Knife
subtitle: Ceremonial flint blade
material: Flaked flint, with organic (ivory or bone) handle on elaborate examples
location: Musée du Louvre, Paris
discovery: Flint knives of this style are known from Predynastic elite burials and settlement finds.
description: A finely worked flint blade produced using a ripple-flaking technique that required great skill, sometimes fitted with a carved handle.
significance: Such knives show the technical mastery of Predynastic flint-working and the emergence of prestige craft goods before the widespread use of metal.

name: Step Pyramid of Djoser
subtitle: Earliest monumental stone pyramid
location: Saqqara, in situ
discovery: Long known and never buried from view; formally investigated and restored through excavations beginning in the early 20th century, notably by Jean-Philippe Lauer.
description: Designed for King Djoser by the official Imhotep, this six-tiered structure is considered the first large-scale cut-stone building in history.
significance: It marks a turning point in Egyptian architecture, establishing stone pyramid-building traditions that led to the later Giza pyramids.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Meidum Geese
subtitle: Tomb wall painting fragment
origin: Mastaba of Nefermaat and Itet, Meidum
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Discovered in 1871 by Luigi Vassalli in the decorated mastaba chapel at Meidum.
description: A finely painted frieze showing six geese, executed with close attention to natural coloring and posture, from the chapel of a high-ranking Old Kingdom official.
significance: It is celebrated as one of the finest surviving examples of Old Kingdom painting and naturalistic depiction of the natural world.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Block Statue of an Official
subtitle: Middle Kingdom private statuary
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Block statues of this form are documented from temple and tomb finds across Middle Kingdom sites.
description: A statue type showing an official seated with knees drawn up and arms folded, the body reduced to a simplified cubic mass with the head and inscribed surfaces left detailed.
significance: The block statue became one of the most enduring formats in Egyptian private sculpture, remaining popular for over a thousand years.

name: Funerary Model Boat
subtitle: Wooden tomb model
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Model boats of this kind were recovered from Middle Kingdom tomb assemblages, notably during Metropolitan Museum expeditions in the early 20th century.
description: A painted wooden model showing a crewed boat, placed in a tomb to allow the deceased to travel symbolically in the afterlife.
significance: Such models illustrate Middle Kingdom funerary beliefs and provide detailed evidence of contemporary boat construction and daily activity.

name: Golden Throne of Tutankhamun
subtitle: Royal ceremonial throne
material: Wood overlaid with gold and silver, inlaid with glass and faience
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Found in 1922 by Howard Carter's team among the furnishings inside the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62).
description: An elaborately decorated wooden throne showing the king and his queen beneath the rays of the sun disk, combining Amarna-period artistic style with royal iconography.
significance: It is one of the finest surviving pieces of Egyptian royal furniture and offers insight into royal imagery near the end of the Amarna period.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Book of the Dead Papyrus (Papyrus of Ani)
subtitle: Illustrated funerary text
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Acquired at Thebes in 1888 by Egyptologist E. A. Wallis Budge on behalf of the British Museum.
description: An illustrated papyrus scroll containing spells and vignettes from the Book of the Dead, prepared for the scribe Ani to guide and protect him in the afterlife.
significance: It is one of the largest and most completely preserved Book of the Dead papyri, providing extensive evidence for New Kingdom funerary belief.

name: Colossi of Memnon
subtitle: Monumental royal statues
location: Thebes necropolis, in situ
discovery: Never buried or lost; the statues have stood at the site since antiquity and were widely visited by Greek and Roman travelers.
description: Two massive seated statues of King Amenhotep III that once flanked the entrance to his mortuary temple, of which little else survives.
significance: The colossi are among the largest freestanding statues from the ancient world and remain a landmark of the Theban necropolis.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Bronze Situla of Isis
subtitle: Ritual libation vessel
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Vessels of this type are known from temple deposits and votive offerings of the Ptolemaic period.
description: A bucket-shaped ritual vessel decorated with religious imagery, used to pour liquid offerings such as milk or water during temple ceremonies honoring Isis.
significance: Situlae illustrate the continuation of traditional Egyptian temple ritual under Ptolemaic (Greek-descended) rule.

name: Fayum Mummy Portrait
subtitle: Naturalistic funerary portrait
material: Encaustic (pigment in wax) on wood panel
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Panels of this type were recovered from cemetery sites in the Fayum region, especially through excavations in the late 19th century.
description: A lifelike painted portrait attached to the wrapped mummy of the deceased, blending Roman painting technique with Egyptian mummification practice.
significance: Fayum portraits are among the best-preserved paintings to survive from the ancient world and document the fusion of Egyptian, Greek and Roman culture.

name: Temple of Kalabsha
subtitle: Roman-period Egyptian temple
location: Relocated to New Kalabsha, near Aswan
discovery: Dismantled and relocated stone-by-stone in the 1960s–70s to save it from flooding after the construction of the Aswan High Dam.
description: A sandstone temple dedicated to the Nubian god Mandulis, built in traditional Egyptian temple form during the early Roman administration of Egypt.
significance: It shows the continuation of Egyptian temple architecture and religious practice under Roman rule, and was the subject of a major international rescue effort.

name: Ivory Comb of King Djet
subtitle: Early royal ivory carving
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Excavated from an Early Dynastic royal tomb context at Abydos.
description: A small ivory comb topped with a carved scene showing the king's name and imagery associated with kingship and the sky, from the reign of King Djet.
significance: It is an early example of combining royal name inscriptions with symbolic imagery, reflecting the formation of pharaonic visual traditions.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Middle Kingdom Cartonnage Coffin
subtitle: Painted funerary coffin
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Recovered from Middle Kingdom provincial cemeteries excavated in the early 20th century.
description: A rectangular wooden coffin painted with bands of funerary text and a pair of protective eyes, typical of Middle Kingdom provincial burial practice.
significance: Coffins of this type preserve some of the earliest extensive versions of funerary spells later collected into the Book of the Dead.

name: Badarian Ivory Figurine
subtitle: Early female figurine
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Recovered from Badarian cemetery excavations in the early 20th century, among the earliest Egyptian culture groups studied.
description: A small carved ivory figure representing the human form in a simplified, stylized manner, typical of the earliest known Egyptian sculpture.
significance: Figurines like this represent some of the oldest surviving examples of Egyptian figural art, predating the unification of Egypt by well over a thousand years.

name: Naqada I Black-Topped Red Ware Vessel
subtitle: Fired pottery jar
material: Fired Nile clay, black-topped red ware
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Excavated from Predynastic cemetery sites in Upper Egypt.
description: A polished red pottery vessel with a distinctive black rim, produced by controlling the firing atmosphere — one of the most recognizable pottery styles of the Naqada I period.
significance: This ware type helped archaeologists first establish a relative chronology for Predynastic Egypt.

name: Fish-Shaped Cosmetic Palette
subtitle: Animal-form grinding palette
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Found in Predynastic burials, where such palettes were common grave goods.
description: A flat siltstone palette carved in the shape of a fish, used for grinding mineral pigments such as malachite for cosmetic use.
significance: Animal-shaped palettes show the early development of Egyptian decorative and symbolic art traditions before the dynastic period.

name: Predynastic Bone Comb
subtitle: Personal grooming implement
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Combs of this type are known from Predynastic cemetery finds.
description: A simple carved bone comb, sometimes topped with a carved animal figure, used for hair care and occasionally placed in burials.
significance: Such everyday objects offer insight into personal care practices in Predynastic communities.

name: Statue of King Khasekhemwy
subtitle: Royal jubilee statue
location: Ashmolean Museum, Oxford
discovery: Excavated in 1898 by James Quibell at Hierakonpolis.
description: A seated statue of King Khasekhemwy wearing the White Crown of Upper Egypt, one of the earliest known royal statues carved in stone.
significance: It marks an important stage in the development of Egyptian royal statuary at the close of the Early Dynastic Period.

name: Stela of King Djet ("Serpent King")
subtitle: Royal funerary stela
location: Musée du Louvre, Paris
discovery: Excavated in 1900 by Émile Amélineau at the royal necropolis of Abydos.
description: A large carved stela bearing the serekh (name panel) of King Djet, surmounted by the Horus falcon, originally erected at the king's tomb.
significance: It is one of the finest surviving examples of Early Dynastic relief carving and royal name iconography.

name: Scorpion Macehead
subtitle: Ceremonial macehead
location: Ashmolean Museum, Oxford
discovery: Excavated in 1897–1898 by James Quibell at the main deposit of the temple at Hierakonpolis, alongside the Narmer Palette.
description: A large ceremonial macehead carved with registers of figures and a scorpion symbol beside a royal figure, from the final stage before Egypt's unification.
significance: It is a key source for debates about the identity of very early rulers and the process of state formation in Egypt.

name: Ivory Label of King Aha
subtitle: Inscribed identification label
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Small labels of this kind were found attached to grave goods in Early Dynastic royal and elite tombs.
description: A small ivory tag inscribed with early hieroglyphic signs recording the name of King Aha and details of goods it was once attached to.
significance: Labels like this are among the earliest surviving examples of Egyptian writing used for record-keeping.

name: Statue of Khafre Enthroned
subtitle: Royal diorite statue
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Excavated in 1860 by Auguste Mariette in the Valley Temple of Khafre at Giza.
description: A statue showing King Khafre seated on a throne with the falcon god Horus protecting his head, carved from extremely hard diorite stone.
significance: It is considered one of the finest examples of Old Kingdom royal sculpture and idealized kingship imagery.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Triad of Menkaure
subtitle: King with goddesses group statue
location: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
discovery: Excavated between 1908 and 1910 by a Harvard University–Museum of Fine Arts expedition led by George Reisner.
description: A statue group showing King Menkaure flanked by the goddess Hathor and a personification of an Egyptian province, exemplifying Old Kingdom triadic composition.
significance: Several such triads were found together, providing rich evidence for royal religious and provincial symbolism under Menkaure.

name: Great Pyramid of Khufu
subtitle: Royal pyramid tomb
location: Giza Plateau, in situ
discovery: Never lost to history; the interior chambers have been explored and documented since antiquity and studied extensively since the 19th century.
description: The largest of the Giza pyramids, built as the tomb of King Khufu and originally cased in polished white limestone.
significance: It is the only surviving structure among the ancient Seven Wonders of the World and a landmark of Old Kingdom engineering.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Mastaba Relief of Ti
subtitle: Tomb chapel wall relief
location: Saqqara, in situ
discovery: The mastaba of Ti was excavated by Auguste Mariette in the 1860s and remains one of the best-preserved Old Kingdom tomb chapels.
description: Detailed relief scenes from the tomb chapel of the official Ti, showing agriculture, boat-building, and daily estate activities.
significance: The reliefs are among the richest visual sources for understanding everyday life and labor in Old Kingdom Egypt.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Old Kingdom Reserve Head
subtitle: Smooth funerary portrait head
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Reserve heads of this type were found in shaft tombs at Giza during early 20th-century excavations.
description: A smoothly finished limestone head, without a body, placed in the burial shaft of a tomb rather than the chapel above — a distinctive Old Kingdom funerary sculpture type.
significance: Scholars debate their exact purpose, but they are thought to have served as a substitute image of the deceased for the afterlife.

name: Pyramid Texts of Unas
subtitle: Earliest religious inscriptions
material: Carved and painted stone (in situ wall inscription)
location: Saqqara, in situ
discovery: First recorded by Gaston Maspero in 1881 when he entered the burial chamber of the Pyramid of Unas.
description: A collection of religious spells carved into the interior walls of King Unas's pyramid, intended to protect and guide the king in the afterlife.
significance: These are the oldest known corpus of Egyptian religious writing, and the direct ancestor of the later Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Faience Hippopotamus ("William")
subtitle: Painted funerary figurine
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Excavated from a Middle Kingdom tomb at Meir in the early 20th century.
description: A small blue-glazed faience figurine of a hippopotamus decorated with painted lotus-flower motifs, a well-known type of Middle Kingdom tomb object.
significance: Hippo figurines like this reflect Egyptian beliefs about rebirth and the dangerous-but-protective symbolism of the animal in funerary contexts.

name: Statue of Senusret III
subtitle: Royal portrait sculpture
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Statues of Senusret III have been recovered from several Middle Kingdom temple sites.
description: A royal statue notable for its unusually careful, aged facial features rather than idealized youth, showing the king with a weary, watchful expression.
significance: The realistic portraiture of Senusret III marks a distinctive shift in how Middle Kingdom rulers chose to be represented.

name: Sphinx of Amenemhat III
subtitle: Royal sphinx statue
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Found at Tanis, where it had been moved and reinscribed by later rulers, but stylistically dated to the Middle Kingdom.
description: A granite sphinx combining a lion's body with a human royal face, showing the strong, fleshy features characteristic of Amenemhat III's portraiture.
significance: It illustrates both the artistic style of the late Middle Kingdom and the common later Egyptian practice of reusing older royal statues.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Middle Kingdom Cosmetic Spoon
subtitle: Decorative toiletry object
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Cosmetic spoons of this style are known from Middle Kingdom tomb assemblages.
description: An elegantly carved spoon, often shaped like a swimming figure holding a shallow bowl, used to hold cosmetic oils or unguents.
significance: Such objects show the high level of craftsmanship applied to everyday personal items in the Middle Kingdom.

name: Papyrus Westcar
subtitle: Collection of literary tales
location: Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection, Berlin
discovery: Acquired in the 19th century; the exact excavation findspot is not documented.
description: A papyrus preserving a set of stories told to King Khufu, including tales of magic and wonder, written in the hieratic script.
significance: It is one of the earliest surviving examples of Egyptian narrative literature written for entertainment rather than religious or administrative purposes.

name: Rock-Cut Tombs of Beni Hasan
subtitle: Provincial governors' tomb complex
location: Beni Hasan, in situ
discovery: Known and studied since the early 19th century, with detailed recording carried out by Percy Newberry in the 1890s.
description: A row of rock-cut tomb chapels belonging to provincial governors, decorated with painted scenes of daily life, hunting, and wrestling.
significance: The tombs are a major source for Middle Kingdom provincial administration, art, and social life outside the royal court.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Kneeling Statue of Hatshepsut
subtitle: Female pharaoh's royal statue
origin: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Excavated by the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Egyptian expedition in the early 20th century.
description: A large granite statue showing Hatshepsut, one of the few female pharaohs, kneeling and presenting offering jars, depicted with traditional royal male regalia.
significance: Statues like this reflect how Hatshepsut used established pharaonic imagery to assert her legitimacy as ruler.

name: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut
subtitle: Terraced temple complex
location: Deir el-Bahari, in situ
discovery: Studied and restored across multiple archaeological missions beginning in the 19th century, notably by the Egypt Exploration Fund and later Polish-Egyptian teams.
description: A terraced temple built into the cliffs at Deir el-Bahari, designed by the architect Senenmut and decorated with scenes including Hatshepsut's expedition to the Land of Punt.
significance: It is considered one of the architectural masterpieces of the New Kingdom and a key monument of Hatshepsut's reign.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Colossal Statue of Akhenaten
subtitle: Amarna-style royal colossus
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Excavated at Karnak by French archaeologist Henri Chevrier in the 1920s–30s.
description: A colossal statue of King Akhenaten carved in the distinctive elongated, stylized manner of early Amarna art, from his temple to the sun-disk Aten at Karnak.
significance: It exemplifies the radical shift in royal representation introduced during Akhenaten's religious reforms.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Amarna Letters Tablet
subtitle: Diplomatic cuneiform correspondence
location: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin / The British Museum, London
discovery: Discovered by local residents in 1887 at the site of Amarna, in the ruins of the royal archive building.
description: A clay tablet inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform, part of a cache of diplomatic letters exchanged between the Egyptian court and rulers of the ancient Near East.
significance: The Amarna Letters are a major source for understanding international relations, trade, and diplomacy in the Late Bronze Age.

name: Ushabti of Tutankhamun
subtitle: Funerary servant figure
origin: Tomb of Tutankhamun, Valley of the Kings
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Found in 1922 by Howard Carter's team; over 400 ushabti figures were included among the tomb's funerary equipment.
description: A carved and painted wooden figure representing the king, intended to magically perform labor on his behalf in the afterlife.
significance: The large number of ushabtis found in the tomb illustrates the scale of funerary provisioning expected for a New Kingdom pharaoh.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Abu Simbel Temple of Ramesses II
subtitle: Rock-cut temple complex
location: Abu Simbel, in situ (relocated)
discovery: Rediscovered by European travelers in 1813 after being buried in sand; famously relocated in the 1960s in a UNESCO-led rescue from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.
description: A monumental rock-cut temple fronted by four colossal seated statues of Ramesses II, built to commemorate his reign and assert Egyptian power over Nubia.
significance: Its relocation to save it from flooding became a landmark international heritage preservation effort and led to the founding of UNESCO's World Heritage program.

name: Younger Memnon (Statue of Ramesses II)
subtitle: Colossal royal head and torso
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Removed from the Ramesseum in 1816 under the direction of Giovanni Belzoni and shipped to England.
description: A colossal granite bust of Ramesses II, part of a larger seated statue that once stood at his mortuary temple, the Ramesseum.
significance: Its dramatic removal and arrival in London helped spark 19th-century European fascination with ancient Egypt, and it reportedly inspired Percy Bysshe Shelley's poem 'Ozymandias.'

name: Papyrus of Hunefer
subtitle: Illustrated Book of the Dead scroll
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Acquired by the British Museum in the 19th century as part of its growing Egyptian papyrus collection.
description: An illustrated funerary papyrus prepared for the scribe Hunefer, famous for its vividly painted 'Weighing of the Heart' judgment scene.
significance: It is one of the most frequently reproduced Book of the Dead vignettes, illustrating core New Kingdom beliefs about judgment in the afterlife.

name: Amarna Princesses Relief
subtitle: Royal family scene fragment
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Recovered from house and temple ruins at Amarna during excavations in the early 20th century.
description: A relief fragment showing two of Akhenaten and Nefertiti's daughters seated affectionately together, typical of the informal family scenes favored in Amarna art.
significance: Such reliefs are notable for their unusually intimate, naturalistic portrayal of royal family life compared to earlier, more formal Egyptian art.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Temple of Philae
subtitle: Temple complex of Isis
location: Agilkia Island, near Aswan (relocated)
discovery: Dismantled and relocated to Agilkia Island in the 1970s–80s as part of a UNESCO-led rescue from flooding caused by the Aswan High Dam.
description: A temple complex dedicated primarily to the goddess Isis, built and expanded over centuries spanning the late Pharaonic through Ptolemaic and Roman periods.
significance: It was one of the last active centers of ancient Egyptian religion, with temple worship continuing there into the 6th century CE.

name: Statue of Queen Arsinoe II
subtitle: Ptolemaic royal statue
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Statues of Arsinoe II have been recovered from Ptolemaic-period temple and city sites in Egypt.
description: A statue representing Queen Arsinoe II, wife and co-ruler of Ptolemy II, shown in Egyptian royal style with attributes linking her to Egyptian goddesses.
significance: It reflects how the Greek-descended Ptolemaic rulers adopted traditional Egyptian royal and religious imagery to legitimize their rule.

name: Canopus Decree Stela
subtitle: Trilingual priestly decree
location: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Discovered in 1866 near the town of Tanta, predating the Rosetta Stone's decipherment role but sharing its trilingual format.
description: A decree issued by a council of Egyptian priests honoring Ptolemy III, inscribed in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek scripts.
significance: Because it uses the same three-script format as the Rosetta Stone, it independently helped confirm and refine the decipherment of hieroglyphs.
sourceName: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

name: Gayer-Anderson Cat
subtitle: Bronze statuette of a sacred cat
material: Cast bronze with gold nose ring and earrings
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Donated to the British Museum in 1939 by Major Robert Gayer-Anderson, after whom it is named.
description: A finely cast bronze statuette of a seated cat, adorned with jewelry, associated with the cult of the cat goddess Bastet.
significance: It is one of the best-known examples of Egyptian animal-cult bronze statuary and a popular symbol of ancient Egyptian religion in modern culture.

name: Ptolemaic Faience Amulet of Bes
subtitle: Protective household amulet
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Amulets of this type are common finds from Late Period through Ptolemaic settlement and burial sites.
description: A small glazed amulet in the form of the dwarf god Bes, worn or displayed for protection against evil, especially for households and childbirth.
significance: Bes amulets remained popular across many periods of Egyptian history, showing the continuity of protective folk religion.

name: Temple of Dendur
subtitle: Roman-period Egyptian temple
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Dismantled and relocated in the 1960s to save it from flooding by the Aswan High Dam; given to the United States by Egypt and reconstructed at the Met in 1978.
description: A small sandstone temple built under Roman rule and dedicated to the goddess Isis and two deified sons of a local Nubian chieftain.
significance: It is a rare example of an intact ancient Egyptian temple on display outside Egypt, illustrating the continuation of Egyptian temple-building traditions under Rome.

name: Roman Provincial Coin of Egypt
subtitle: Alexandrian bronze coin
location: The British Museum, London
discovery: Coins of this type are common archaeological finds throughout Roman Egypt.
description: A bronze coin struck at the Alexandria mint, combining Roman imperial portraiture with distinctly Egyptian religious imagery on the reverse.
significance: Provincial coinage like this shows how Roman administration blended with local Egyptian religious and cultural identity.

name: Shroud with Portrait of a Woman
subtitle: Painted funerary shroud
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Painted shrouds of this kind were recovered from Roman-period cemetery sites in Egypt.
description: A full-length painted linen shroud showing the deceased in fine dress and jewelry, flanked by Egyptian funerary deities such as Anubis and Osiris.
significance: It shows the blending of Roman-style portraiture with traditional Egyptian funerary iconography in this period.

name: Statuette of Serapis
subtitle: Syncretic deity figure
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Statuettes of Serapis are known from temple and household contexts across Roman Egypt and the wider Mediterranean.
description: A statuette of Serapis, a syncretic god combining Egyptian (Osiris-Apis) and Greek attributes, promoted especially in Alexandria.
significance: The cult of Serapis illustrates the religious blending characteristic of Ptolemaic and Roman-period Egypt, and it spread widely across the Roman world.

name: Roman-Period Osiris-Canopus Jar
subtitle: Composite religious vessel
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Vessels of this composite type are known from Roman-period temple deposits in Egypt.
description: A vessel combining the form of a canopic-style jar with the head of the god Osiris, used in rituals associated with the annual Nile flood and Osirian mysteries.
significance: It reflects distinctly Roman-period developments in Osirian religious practice within Egypt.

name: Pectoral of Senusret II
subtitle: Inlaid royal pendant
material: Gold inlaid with carnelian, lapis lazuli, turquoise, and garnet
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York / Egyptian Museum, Cairo
discovery: Excavated in 1914 by Flinders Petrie's team in the pyramid complex of Senusret II at El-Lahun.
description: An elaborately inlaid gold pectoral naming Senusret II, showing falcons flanking his throne name, from the treasure of Princess Sithathoriunet.
significance: It represents the peak of Middle Kingdom goldworking and inlay craftsmanship.

name: New Kingdom Broad Collar (Wesekh)
subtitle: Multi-strand ceremonial necklace
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Broad collars of this type have been recovered from New Kingdom tomb assemblages, including non-royal burials.
description: A wide, multi-row collar made of small colorful beads terminating in falcon-head clasps, worn for both daily adornment and burial.
significance: The wesekh collar was one of the most widespread and recognizable forms of ancient Egyptian jewelry, worn across social classes.

name: New Kingdom Electrum Earrings
subtitle: Royal or elite jewelry pair
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Earrings of this type appear in elite New Kingdom tomb finds; pierced ears become more common in Egyptian fashion during this period.
description: A pair of hoop-style earrings made from electrum, reflecting the growing New Kingdom fashion for elaborate personal jewelry influenced partly by contact with neighboring cultures.
significance: They illustrate changing New Kingdom fashions in body adornment compared to earlier periods.

name: Middle Kingdom Amethyst Scarab Ring
subtitle: Inscribed signet ring
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Rings of this style are documented from Middle Kingdom elite burials.
description: A gold ring set with a carved amethyst scarab, the base inscribed with a name or motto, worn both as jewelry and as a personal seal.
significance: Scarab rings combined decorative, religious, and practical administrative functions in Middle Kingdom elite life.

name: Old Kingdom Copper Adze
subtitle: Woodworking tool
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Copper tools of this kind are known from Old Kingdom settlement and tomb-model contexts.
description: A woodworking tool with a curved copper blade bound to a wooden handle, used for shaping timber in construction and craft production.
significance: Copper tools like this mark the technological shift from purely stone-based toolkits and supported Old Kingdom monumental building projects.

name: New Kingdom Bronze Sickle
subtitle: Agricultural harvesting tool
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Bronze sickles of this type are known from New Kingdom settlement and tomb-model finds.
description: A curved bronze blade used for harvesting grain, reflecting the increasing use of bronze tools in New Kingdom agriculture.
significance: Agricultural tools like this underline the central importance of grain farming to the Egyptian economy.

name: New Kingdom Ostracon Sketch
subtitle: Informal artist's sketch
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Large numbers of ostraca were recovered from the workmen's village of Deir el-Medina, home to the artisans who built the royal tombs.
description: A quick sketch or study, often humorous or informal, painted on a flake of limestone by a New Kingdom artist practicing figures or animals.
significance: Ostraca like this offer a rare, informal glimpse into the working lives and even the humor of ancient Egyptian craftsmen.

name: New Kingdom Wooden Headrest
subtitle: Sleeping support object
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Headrests of this type are common finds in New Kingdom tombs, used both in life and included as burial goods.
description: A curved wooden support used in place of a pillow, resting under the neck while sleeping, sometimes carved with protective deities.
significance: Headrests illustrate everyday Egyptian domestic furniture and were believed to offer symbolic protection during sleep, likened to a form of nightly 'rebirth.'

name: New Kingdom Senet Game Board
subtitle: Board game with playing pieces
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Senet boards are known from numerous New Kingdom tomb finds, including from the tomb of Tutankhamun.
description: A game board with a 30-square grid used for the popular board game senet, played with carved playing pieces and throw-sticks or knucklebones.
significance: Senet was both a common leisure activity and, in later belief, symbolically linked to the deceased's journey through the afterlife.

name: New Kingdom Kohl Container
subtitle: Cosmetic eye-paint holder
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Kohl containers are frequent finds in New Kingdom tombs of both men and women.
description: A small carved vessel used to store kohl, the dark mineral-based eye cosmetic worn by Egyptian men and women for both decorative and practical (sun-glare, insect) reasons.
significance: Everyday cosmetic objects like this highlight the broad social practice of eye-painting across ancient Egyptian society.

name: Old Kingdom Bread Mold
subtitle: Ceramic baking vessel
location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
discovery: Large numbers of bread molds have been found at Old Kingdom bakery and settlement sites, notably near the pyramid workers' town at Giza.
description: A tall, conical pottery mold used to bake the bread that formed a staple part of the ancient Egyptian diet and temple food offerings.
significance: Bread mold finds have helped archaeologists understand the large-scale food production needed to support pyramid-building workforces.
